captions.text: Start in Department Settings.
Open Calls & Dispatch and choose Call & Dispatch Settings.
This lesson follows the complete setup of a Personnel check-in rule,
then tests it on one fictional call.
Check-ins help coordinators organize agreed reporting updates, including
community care visits and mental health response assignments.
Department administrators configure the rules; operators use the
resulting timers and history.

scenes.title: Choose automatic or per-call enablement

captions.text: Find Check-In Timer Settings.
Auto-Enable Check-In Timers for New Calls controls whether new

captions.text: calls start with timers enabled.
It is off in this training department.
We leave it off and explicitly enable one practice call later.
This separates department-wide enablement from the reporting

captions.text: Under Add New Default Timer, choose Personnel as the Target Type.
Set Duration to thirty minutes and Warning Threshold to five minutes.
Leave Enabled selected.
Active States can restrict when a timer applies; leaving it empty uses All States.
Review the values, then select Add Timer Config.
Use intervals and state filters that your department has agreed for its work.

scenes.title: Verify the saved default and its impact

captions.text: Verify the saved Personnel row in Default Timer Configurations: thirty
minutes, a five-minute warning threshold, Enabled Yes, and Active States All.
This default applies when an enabled timer has no matching override.
The warning threshold defines how close to the due time the
server marks a timer as Warning.
Here that window is the final five minutes of the thirty-minute interval.
An overdue timer has reached its reporting deadline.
Check the resulting behavior in the applications your department uses.

captions.text: Use Add New Override for a rule tied to a call type or priority.
Here Call Type ID is Rescue, Call Priority is Any, Target Type is
Personnel, Duration is forty-five minutes, and Warning Threshold is ten.
We clear Enabled to save this example in a disabled state.
Active States is empty.
Select Add Override after reviewing the scope and values.

scenes.title: Compare saved overrides with the default

captions.text: Review Call Type / Priority Overrides.
The Rescue row now shows forty-five minutes, ten warning minutes, and
Enabled No, so that example is inactive.
The existing Investigation Personnel rule is enabled for sixty minutes
with a five-minute warning threshold.
Matching enabled overrides take precedence over the default.
We will use Investigation to test that sixty-minute rule while
retaining the thirty-minute default.

Our type is Investigation and the priority is Routine.
The Call Identifier gives this exercise another recognizable reference.
Keep the scenario fictional and identify it clearly so other operators
can distinguish it from normal work.
We use a supplied fictional location for this software exercise.

Review the selected row rather than assuming a station, role, or group
contains the intended recipient.
For a real rollout, test with an agreed training audience first.
A call may have several participants, so the recipient scope matters when you
review which personnel timers appear.

scenes.title: Enable timers for the individual call

captions.text: Near the bottom of the form, select Enable Check-In Timers.
This is the per-call choice we planned while automatic enablement remained off.
Review the rest of the call and its recipients, then choose
Create and Dispatch Call.
Saving timer configuration alone does not opt this call into
timers; this checkbox makes that choice explicit for the exercise.

scenes.title: Verify the override on the live call

captions.text: Open the new call and inspect Check-In Timers.
Wallace Boden has a Personnel timer, the state is OK, and Time Remaining
is just under sixty minutes.
This call uses the enabled Investigation override rather
than the thirty-minute default.
Open Show Check-In History to inspect the saved entries; this
new exercise initially has none.
This readback checks the effect of the configuration on an actual call.

captions.text: The Check In dialog provides a Note field.
Enter a concise update under your department procedure,
review it, and select Check In.
Our note identifies a software practice check-in for this timer lesson.
It makes no claim about physical arrival or device location.
The note belongs to the check-in record, so it should explain
the update clearly enough for another coordinator to understand.

captions.text: Review the timer and saved history after confirmation.
The table shows Timestamp, Who, Type, and Note.
Our new Personnel entry contains the exact practice note we entered.
The timer has begun a new interval.
Checking the saved history distinguishes a completed update
from text left in a dialog.
Keep status reporting, check-in reporting, and any physical safety verification under
their appropriate department procedures.

captions.text: Finish the exercise through Close Call.
Review Completed Type, Send Notification, and Completed Notes.
We use Closed, leave Send Notification off for this local practice, and
record a clear completion note.
Then select Close Call.
Review these choices for your own audience: the notification option
changes whether the closing event is sent to the call participants.

scenes.title: Verify closure and retain the history

captions.text: Verify that the call now shows Closed and the expected Completed Notes.
Its saved check-in history remains available for review.
The same configuration and verification habits apply to search and rescue,
security companies, wildland contractors, and industrial response teams: choose
the reporting target, agree the interval, test the matching rule,
and check the resulting record before extending the setup to everyday work.
